newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU faces barley subsidy tussle with exporters.
newsitem.headline: EU faces barley subsidy tussle with exporters.

text.p: The European Union is under growing pressure to grant higher export subsidies for barley as traders scramble to finalise contracts clinched with Saudi Arabia or face penalties for delivery delays.
But the Commission, torn between helping cover a large barley sale to a major world importer and keeping domestic prices under control, has so far resisted their demands.
Traders estimate that in the face of falling world prices, last week's EU refund of 31 Ecus tonne was insufficient to cover the sale to the Saudis and instead urged at least 35 Ecus.
"We need 35 Ecus to export European barley," one exporter said.
Exporters sold 1.4 million tonnes of barley to Saudi Arabia in late September for $146-$158 a tonne, including freight.
Saudi Arabia needed 200,000 tonnes for delivery in October, 800,000 in November and 400,000 in the first half of December.
The EU, which enjoys a freight and supply advantage over other world suppliers, was initially expected to supply 700,000 tonnes of barley, including 500,000 tonnes from the free market.
Besides the EU, Canada was expected to supply 200-400,000 tonnes, the United States half that amount while Turkey had already sold 125,000 tonnes. Australia was also expected to do some cargoes.
But exporters now put the EU share in the Saudi contract at 800,000 to 900,000 tonnes, citing logistics and climate problems experienced by other potential suppliers.
The Commission has already helped cover part of the EU contract but traders estimate exporters are still short.
They said time was running out, particularly for barley shipments due in November.
"It is clear there is an important short in the market. It is a race against the clock," one trader said.
Last week traders bid through France to export some 636,000 tonnes of free market barley at subsidies ranging from 31.00 to 39.97 Ecus per tonne.
But the EU only awarded 30,000 tonnes at 31 Ecus, making the sale worth $130 per tonne, FOB UK.
Traders said their margin for manoeuvre was very small as the Commission wants to keep domestic barley prices in check and is also aware exporters are in a tight spot.
"The problem is that Commission knows there is still an important short in the market," one trader said.
But exporters hope the EU may finally relent to avoid missing on future contracts with the Saudis.
"If the EU wants to participate in the next sale to the Saudis, it must follow world prices," one exporter said.

Barley is currently worth some $125 per tonne on world markets. Traders, who saw bids for licences rejected last week, are expected to bid massively again at this week's tenders. --Paris newsroom +331 4221 5432
